paras: The attack on Deb Flynn in Marinette was a mob assault on a Black hotel porter at a street carnival in Marinette, Wisconsin, on the night of July 9, 1903, after white men objected to his walking with a white girl. Flynn escaped a crowd armed with hammers, was hidden overnight and was taken out of town the next day. The Associated Press carried the story nationally, and Southern papers used it to mock the North and to say the white girl deserved punishment.

Marinette was holding a street carnival in July 1903 that a special dispatch called a "military carnival." Company I of the Second Regiment, Wisconsin National Guard, attended in a body, and some of its members served as police on the grounds. According to a Menominee, Michigan, report in the Minneapolis Journal, Flynn was a porter at the Marinette hotel.

In that account, Flynn was walking the grounds with white friends, among them two or three girls, when a showman at a cane stand made insulting remarks about a "nigger" walking with a white girl. When Flynn asked whom he meant, the showman answered "I mean you" and swung a hammer at his head, but one of Flynn's white friends struck the showman in the face and knocked him down. Held back by the carnival police, the showman raised the cry of "Hey Rube," his fellow showmen gathered, and Company I members ran to the scene. Flynn got over a fence and escaped toward town, followed for some distance by the showman and several others.

The Associated Press dispatch, dated July 10, told it differently: Flynn "got into a quarrel with some Southerners" who resented his walking with a white girl, a carnival crowd collected, and "clubs, stones and hammers were used on the negro." In this version militia rescued him; he was hidden overnight and "spirited out of town," "bruised and cut" or, in one summary, "severely beaten."

A special dispatch in the Wisconsin Weekly Advocate said a mob of about twenty carnival employees attacked him and that he "would have been killed, had he not escaped just in time." The same dispatch said the mob also vowed vengeance on a white man who had struck a showman, but he too escaped.
No report of arrests, charges or an inquiry appears in the coverage, and no later word of Flynn was found.

The only Black-press report found, in the Wisconsin Weekly Advocate, ran under the headline "Race Riot at Carnival." It named no victim, called the affair a "small race riot," and laid it to "employees of a carnival company" without further comment. The Minneapolis Journal's Menominee report, headed "Hey Rube," likewise made the showman the aggressor and never mentioned Southerners.

White papers ran the Associated Press version from July 11 under headlines such as "Her Escort a Negro" (Raleigh News and Observer) and "Jump on a Negro" (Saint Paul Globe). Later copies appeared as "Drove Negro from Town" in the Monroe City Democrat of Missouri and "Troops Rescue a Negro" in Wisconsin's Eagle River Review.

In the South the story became editorial material: the Batesburg Advocate of South Carolina headed it "Negro Was Too Bold," and the Richmond Times Dispatch remarked that the Wisconsin town "did not fail to charge it up to 'some southerners.'" The Dawson News of Georgia wrote that "the woman was the party who needed punishment," and the Southern Sentinel of Winnfield, Louisiana, said the girl "should have been accorded the same treatment as the negro." The Gainesville Star went further, listing Wisconsin with Illinois and Indiana as states where a mob had "lynched a negro," a claim no news report of the Marinette attack supports.

The accounts differ on the attackers: the Associated Press named "some Southerners," while the Journal and the Advocate, both from nearer the scene, blamed carnival showmen. The wire also said he was beaten and rescued by the militia (one copy naming Company G of the First regiment), while the Journal said a friend stopped the hammer blow and Flynn escaped over a fence.
The July 10 dispatches place the attack on the night of July 9, but two papers put it on Friday, July 10.

reader.title: Attack on Deb Flynn in Marinette
bases: A crowd of showmen or white men chased and, by the wire account, beat Flynn with clubs, stones and hammers at a carnival; he survived and was taken out of town (A1, A2, A7).

Every account has Flynn surviving, bruised or by escaping, and taken out of town, so no one was killed (A2, A7); the crowd of about twenty acted without authority over his walking with a white girl, which makes it an attempted lynching at most (A1, A8).
The AP dispatch (A2), the Advocate's separate special dispatch (A1) and the Menominee report in the Minneapolis Journal (A7) independently describe the same attack at the Marinette carnival.

accounts.gist: Carnival-company employees, a mob of about twenty, attacked an unnamed Negro walking with a white girl; he would have been killed had he not escaped.

framing.detail: Headed 'Race Riot at Carnival'; places blame on 'employees of a carnival company' without comment.
Wire copies under heads like 'Her Escort a Negro', 'Jump on a Negro', 'Troops Rescue a Negro', 'Drove Negro from Town'.
Southern papers headed it 'Negro Was Too Bold' and 'It Wouldn't Do' and said the white girl deserved punishment.
The Richmond Times Dispatch and Gainesville Star used the story to jab at the North for blaming 'some southerners' and for its mobs.
The Minneapolis Journal's Menominee report told the incident as a carnival brawl under 'Hey Rube', with the showman as aggressor.
